title: Binary addition, shifts and hexadecimal
specPoints: **Add** two 8-bit binary integers and explain **overflow** errors which may occur
**Binary shifts** left and right, their effect of multiplying and dividing by 2, and loss of precision
Convert **denary 0–255 to and from 2-digit hexadecimal**, and **binary to and from hexadecimal**
learn: Add two 8-bit binary numbers using the four column rules and carries
Recognise an overflow error and explain why it happens in 8 bits
Perform a left or right shift and state its effect on the value
Explain why a right shift can lose precision and a left shift can overflow
Convert between denary, binary and hexadecimal in any direction
Explain why programmers use hexadecimal when computers only understand binary
hook: In 1996 a rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch. A number was too big for the space it was stored in: an overflow. Nobody died, but it cost hundreds of millions. Today you will make an overflow happen on paper, see why shifting bits left doubles a number, and learn the colour code #FF8800 is just three bytes in disguise.

video.title: Carry the one, slide the bits, count to F
video.brief: 5 minutes. Part 1: column addition of 10110101 + 01001110 with carries shown bouncing to the next column; then 11000000 + 01000000 where a ninth bit falls off the end: overflow. Part 2: 00001011 (11) slides left one place to 00010110 (22); slides right one place to 00000101 (5), with the lost 1 dropping off the right. Part 3: the 16 hex digits as a lift panel 0–F; split 10110101 into nibbles 1011 and 0101 → B5; then B5 → 11 × 16 + 5 = 181. End: a colour picker showing #FF8800 as three bytes.

p: Binary addition works like denary column addition, but you carry when a column reaches 2 instead of 10. Learn the four rules and write every carry above the next column.

An 8-bit register can hold 0 to 255. If an addition produces a result bigger than 255 it needs a ninth bit, and there is nowhere to put it. The extra bit is lost. This is an **overflow error**: the stored answer is wrong because the result is too large for the number of bits available.

In the example above, a CPU with 8-bit registers would keep only 00000011 = 3 and drop the leading 1. It might set an overflow flag so the program can notice, or it might just continue with the wrong value.
list: Overflow happens when: the result is greater than the largest value the bits can store (255 for 8 bits).
Spot it when: there is a carry out of the leftmost column.
In the exam: write the full 9-bit answer **and** state that the result has overflowed.

p: A **left shift** moves every bit one place to the left and puts a 0 in the empty space on the right. Each place shifted left **multiplies by 2**. A **right shift** moves every bit one place to the right and puts a 0 in on the left. Each place right **divides by 2**.

Shifting right can **lose precision**: any 1 pushed off the right-hand end is discarded, so 13 ÷ 2 becomes 6, not 6.5. Shifting left can **overflow**: a 1 pushed off the left-hand end is lost and the value becomes wrong.
explain.code:
Left shift by 1:   00001011 (11)  ->  00010110 (22)   x2
Left shift by 2:   00001011 (11)  ->  00101100 (44)   x4
Right shift by 1:  00001011 (11)  ->  00000101 (5)    /2, the 1 lost -> 5 not 5.5
Right shift by 2:  00001011 (11)  ->  00000010 (2)    /4, precision lost

Overflow on left shift:
                   11000000 (192) ->  10000000 (128)  should be 384, the
                                                     leading 1 was lost
Rule: shift left n places = multiply by 2^n
      shift right n places = divide by 2^n (dropping remainders)

p: **Hexadecimal** (hex, base 16) uses sixteen digits: 0–9 then A–F, where A = 10 and F = 15. One hex digit is exactly one **nibble** (4 bits), so one byte is always two hex digits. Computers do not use hex; **people** do. A long binary string like 10110101 is hard to read and easy to mistype, while B5 is short and memorable. Hex is used for colour codes, MAC addresses, memory addresses and error codes.
Hex is shorter than binary and easier for humans to read, remember and type, and it converts to binary much more simply than denary does. That sentence is worth two marks.

Binary to hex: split into nibbles, convert each nibble. Hex to binary: write each digit as 4 bits. Denary to hex: divide by 16; the whole number is the first digit, the remainder the second. Hex to denary: first digit × 16, add the second digit. Or go through binary if you prefer.
Add the columns from the right. 0+0=0. 0+1=1. 1+1=0 carry 1. 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Write the carry above the next column.
Eight bits can hold up to 255. If the answer is bigger, there is a ninth bit. There is no room for it. The answer is wrong. This is called overflow.

Shift left: move all bits one place left. Put a 0 on the right. The number doubles. Shift right: move all bits one place right. The number halves. A 1 that falls off the right is lost. That is loss of precision.
Hex has 16 digits: 0 to 9 then A to F. A is 10. F is 15. One hex digit is 4 bits. Two hex digits is one byte. People use hex because it is shorter than binary and easier to read.
simple.code:
binary -> hex:  split into 4s.  1011 0101 -> B 5
hex -> binary:  each digit is 4 bits.  3E -> 0011 1110
denary -> hex:  divide by 16.  181 / 16 = 11 r 5 -> B5
hex -> denary:  first x 16 + second.  B5 = 11x16 + 5 = 181

keyterms.def: An error that happens when the result of a calculation is too large to be stored in the number of bits available.
The 1 passed to the next column when two or three 1s are added.
Moving every bit left or right by a number of places.
Moving bits left, which multiplies the value by 2 for each place.
Moving bits right, which divides the value by 2 for each place.
Information lost when bits fall off the end of a shift, e.g. a right shift discarding a remainder.
Base-16 number system using digits 0–9 and A–F; one digit represents four bits.
Four bits; the amount represented by one hexadecimal digit.

try.title: 5. Overflow, shifts and hex in Python
p: Python integers never overflow, so the code masks the result to 8 bits with `& 0xFF` to copy what a real register does. `<<` and `>>` are the shift operators. `hex()` and `int(text, 16)` convert hex. Run it, then change `a` and `b` to the pairs in Try 2.
try.code:
a = 0b11110000      # 240
b = 0b00011111      # 31
total = a + b
print("true answer:", total, "=", format(total, "b"))
stored = total & 0xFF            # keep only the low 8 bits
print("8-bit register keeps:", format(stored, "08b"), "=", stored)
print("overflow?", total > 255)

n = 11
print("\n11 =", format(n, "08b"))
print("11 << 1 =", format(n << 1, "08b"), "=", n << 1)
print("11 << 2 =", format(n << 2, "08b"), "=", n << 2)
print("11 >> 1 =", format(n >> 1, "08b"), "=", n >> 1, "(11/2 is really 5.5)")

print("\n181 in hex:", hex(181), "  B5 in denary:", int("B5", 16))
for h in ["0F", "10", "7F", "80", "FF"]:
    print(h, "=", int(h, 16), "=", format(int(h, 16), "08b"))

exam.q: Add the binary numbers 10101100 and 01110101. Show your working and give your answer in binary.
model: 100100001 (2). One mark for a method with carries shown and at most one bit wrong.
exam.commentary: 172 + 117 = 289, which needs nine bits. Write all nine. If the question says 'explain the problem', add 'the result is larger than 255 so it overflows 8 bits'. Checking in denary takes 20 seconds and catches most errors.

exam.q: A program stores a value in 8 bits and performs a right shift of two places on 00101101. (a) Give the result. (b) Explain the effect of this shift on the value.
model: (a) 00001011 (1). (b) The value is divided by 4 / halved twice (1); the two 1s shifted off the right are lost so the result is 11 rather than 11.25, a loss of precision (1).
exam.commentary: For (b) name the multiplier (÷4, not just 'smaller') and say **what was lost**. 'It divides by 2' for a two-place shift is a common slip.

exam.q: A web designer writes the colour code #4B9FD2 instead of its binary form. Convert 4B to denary and to binary, and explain why hexadecimal is used for colour codes rather than binary.
model: 4B = 4 × 16 + 11 = 75 (1). 4B = 0100 1011 = 01001011 (1). Hex is shorter / easier for a person to read, remember and type than a 24-bit binary string (1), and it is quick to convert to binary because each hex digit is exactly one nibble (1).
exam.commentary: The explanation must be about **people**, not the computer. 'The computer understands hex better' is wrong and loses both explain marks. The nibble point is the one that separates good answers.

home: Make up two 8-bit numbers that add to more than 255 and two that do not. Add all four pairs, mark which overflow, and check each in denary. Then write your birthday (day and month) as two hex numbers and convert them to binary.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 3 · explain 16 · try 26 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 2
misconceptions: 1 + 1 = 2 written in a binary column. Drill the four rules before any sums.
Dropping the ninth bit silently. Students must write it and name the overflow.
Right shift by two 'divides by 2'. Each place is a factor of 2.
Treating hex as something the CPU uses. Hex is a human shorthand for binary.
say: 'Carry when you reach two, not ten.'
'Left is bigger, right is smaller. Anything that falls off the end is gone for good.'
teacher.skip: Try 3 can be reduced to three rows; Try 5 is optional if the class has done Try 1 and Try 4 well.
differentiation: Support: hex–binary–denary table for 0–15 on the desk; addition questions pre-written in columns with a carry row.
Stretch: explain why a 16-bit register could store the result of 11110000 + 00011111 without error, and work out the largest value it can hold.
